```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(gtsummary)
library(gt)
```


# Prompt 1: gtsummary Capabilities

::: callout-note
## Prompt

In Step 1, you have seen how to create a summary table and modify it for various statistical analyses. Summarize the package's capabilities as explained by the speaker. How may the {gtsummary} benefit you for your school work or career?
:::

## Descriptive Tables with `tbl_summary()`

In Dr. Jung's lecture, `tbl_summary()` is the starting point. It was demonstrated on the `trial` data (200 patients, two chemotherapy drugs).

::: incremental
- It **detects variable types** on its own and picks sensible statistics: median (Q1, Q3) for continuous variables, n (%) for categorical ones.
- It **reports missing values** as "Unknown" rows, so nothing is hidden.
- With `by =`, it splits the table by group (for example, Drug A vs. Drug B).
- `add_overall()` and `add_n()` add the overall column and the sample size per variable.
:::

::: aside
Data: `trial` (gtsummary) and `gss_cat` (forcats), as used in the Step 1 lecture.
:::

## Testing Differences Between Groups

One extra line of code turns a descriptive table into a hypothesis test.

::: fragment
- `add_p()` picks the test automatically: **Wilcoxon rank-sum** for continuous variables and **Pearson's chi-square** for categorical ones.
:::

::: fragment
- `add_difference()` gives a **Welch two-sample t-test**, with the mean difference and 95% confidence interval. I learned to be careful here, because switching to means and SDs still uses Wilcoxon unless I use `add_difference()`.
:::

::: fragment
- `add_q(method = "bonferroni")` adjusts p-values when I run many tests at once.
:::

::: fragment
- `add_difference(adj.vars = ...)` produces an **ANCOVA-style adjusted difference**.
:::

## Cross-Tabulation with `tbl_cross()`

- `tbl_cross()` builds a row-by-column table with totals and row, column, or cell percentages, plus a chi-square p-value from `add_p()`.
- The lecture noted that `tbl_summary()` can also run a chi-square test, but `tbl_cross()` makes the more attractive table. `tbl_summary()` is better when one table mixes several kinds of tests.
- It also worked on survey data (`gss_cat`): marital status by race was significant at p \< .001.

## Regression Tables with `tbl_regression()`

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**One-line model tables**

- Logistic regression (`glm`) shows log-odds, or odds ratios with `exponentiate = TRUE`.
- OLS multiple regression (`lm`) shows betas with 95% CIs.
- Reference rows are included for categorical predictors.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Useful add-ons**

- `add_global_p()` for an overall p-value per variable
- `add_vif()` to check collinearity
- `add_glance_table()` for N, log-likelihood, AIC, BIC
- `tbl_uvregression()` for one-predictor-at-a-time models
:::
:::::

## Customizing and Combining Tables

::: incremental
- **Formatting:** `statistic`, `digits`, `label`, and `missing_text` change what each cell shows.
- **Headers and notes:** `modify_header()`, `modify_spanning_header()`, `modify_footnote()`, and `modify_caption()` make a journal-style table.
- **`as_gt()`:** converts a gtsummary table to a gt object so I can add `tab_header()` titles and subtitles.
- **`tbl_merge()` and `tbl_stack()`:** put tables side by side or on top of each other, for example highway vs. city mileage models.
- **Themes:** `theme_gtsummary_journal()` applies JAMA or *Quarterly Journal of Economics* styles.
:::

::: notes
Everything above comes from the Step 1 lecture note (Jae Jung, "Summary table with gtsummary").
:::

## How gtsummary Benefits Me

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**School work**

- My culminating project (CEP) will need descriptive tables, cross-tabs, and regression tables for survey data. gtsummary does each in a few lines.
- Because the code is reproducible, I can re-run a table when the data changes and avoid copying numbers into a document by hand.
- The same style works for my thesis and any journal submission.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Career in digital marketing**

- Comparing campaign groups (A/B tests, audience segments) uses the same `by =` and `add_p()` workflow as the drug comparison.
- Regression tables can show which factors drive engagement or retention.
- Clean, professional tables make results easy to present to non-technical stakeholders.
:::
:::::

## 2.1 How Does gtsummary Differ from gt and gtExtras?

::: callout-note
## Prompt

How does it differ from gt and gtExtras?
:::

| Package | Main purpose | What I have to do |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **gt** | General grammar of tables for any data frame [@iannone2024gt] | Choose and write every cell, header, and format myself |
| **gtExtras** | Extends gt with extra themes, sparklines, and inline mini-plots | Start with a gt table, then add visual extras |
| **gtsummary** | Statistical summary tables from data or models [@sjoberg2021gtsummary] | Pass in data or a model; it calculates and formats the statistics |

::: fragment
gtsummary was written as a companion to gt. The Step 1 lecture showed that `as_gt()` converts a gtsummary table into a gt object, so I can use both packages in the same table.
:::

# Prompt 3: Cross-Tabulation with CEP Data

::: callout-note
## Prompt

Apply what you learned to your MSDM CEP data. Choose two appropriate variables for cross-tabulation and show if the two variables are associated or not. Use appropriate statistics to test if the two variables are associated. Code, produce the table, and interpret the result.
:::

## The CEP Data I Combined

I merged two Collins College of Hospitality Management (CCHM) files:

- **Retention cohorts:** for each Fall cohort (2018 to 2025), the cohort size and how many students were still enrolled one, two, and three years later.
- **Yearly enrollment by term:** the college's Fall headcount, FTES, and average units for each academic year.

Each cohort was matched to the Fall enrollment figures for the year it entered. Note that these are cohort-level counts, not individual survey responses.

## Step 1: Import the Combined Data

```{r}
#| label: import-data

cep_cohort_data <- read_csv("data/cohort_combined.csv")

glimpse(cep_cohort_data)
```

## Step 2: Expand Counts into One Row per Student

The cross-tab needs one row per student, so I turn the retained and not-retained counts into individual rows.

```{r}
#| label: expand-students

cep_long_counts <- cep_cohort_data |>
  select(cohort_year, retained_1yr, not_retained_1yr)

cep_long_counts <- cep_long_counts |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(retained_1yr, not_retained_1yr),
    names_to = "retention_status",
    values_to = "student_count"
  )

cep_student_data <- cep_long_counts |>
  uncount(weights = student_count)

cep_student_data <- cep_student_data |>
  mutate(cohort_year = factor(cohort_year)) |>
  mutate(
    retention_status = factor(
      retention_status,
      levels = c("retained_1yr", "not_retained_1yr"),
      labels = c("Retained after 1 year", "Not retained")
    )
  )

glimpse(cep_student_data)
```

## Step 3: Cross-Tabulation with a Chi-Square Test

```{r}
#| label: crosstab-table

cep_crosstab_table <- cep_student_data |>
  tbl_cross(
    row = cohort_year,
    col = retention_status,
    percent = "row",
    label = list(
      cohort_year ~ "Entering Cohort",
      retention_status ~ "First-Year Retention"
    )
  )

cep_crosstab_table <- cep_crosstab_table |>
  add_p(test = "chisq.test") |>
  bold_labels()

cep_crosstab_table
```

## Interpretation: Cross-Tabulation

I tested whether entering cohort and first-year retention are associated (N = 642 first-time, full-time freshmen).

::: incremental
- The chi-square test was significant: $\chi^2$(7) = 14.37, p = .045.
- The effect is small (Cramér's V = .15).
- Retention ranged from 76.9% (Fall 2021) to 92.5% (Fall 2024), so some cohorts retained noticeably better than others.
- No expected cell count fell below 5, so the chi-square assumptions hold.
:::

::: notes
Check these numbers against your rendered table before presenting.
:::

For CCHM, retention is not constant from year to year, so the cohort a student enters in is related to whether they return for a second year. The association is modest, and this analysis cannot say why. Candidate explanations such as pandemic-era disruption (the Fall 2021 dip) would need student-level data to test.

# Prompt 4: Multiple Regression with CEP Data

::: callout-note
## Prompt

Using the MSDM CEP data, run multiple regression. The dependent variable can be continuous or dichotomous. Regress a dependent variable on a set of independent variables. Code, produce the table, and interpret the result.
:::

## Step 1: Prepare the Regression Data

The dependent variable is the first-year retention rate (%) of each cohort. The independent variables are the Fall college headcount and the Fall average units per student in the cohort's entry year.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-regression

cep_regression_data <- cep_cohort_data |>
  select(retention_rate_1yr, fall_headcount, fall_avg_units)

glimpse(cep_regression_data)
```

## Step 2: Fit the Model

```{r}
#| label: fit-model

cep_regression_model <- lm(
  formula = retention_rate_1yr ~ fall_headcount + fall_avg_units,
  data = cep_regression_data
)
```

## Step 3: Produce the Regression Table

```{r}
#| label: regression-table

cep_regression_table <- cep_regression_model |>
  tbl_regression(
    intercept = TRUE,
    label = list(
      fall_headcount ~ "Fall college headcount",
      fall_avg_units ~ "Fall average units"
    )
  )

cep_regression_table <- cep_regression_table |>
  add_glance_source_note(include = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, p.value)) |>
  bold_p(t = 0.05) |>
  bold_labels()

cep_regression_table
```

## Interpretation: Multiple Regression

::: incremental
- The model was not significant: F(2, 5) = 0.45, p = .66, R² = .15, adjusted R² = −.19.
- Neither predictor was significant: Fall headcount (b = 0.005, p = .74) and Fall average units (b = −8.17, p = .50).
- With only eight cohorts, the model has very little statistical power.
:::

Within these data, I cannot show that college size or student course load explains differences in first-year retention across cohorts. This is a limitation of the data, not proof of no relationship. Fall headcount also tracks cohort size closely (r = .83) and FTES almost perfectly (r = .999), so I used only headcount to avoid collinearity. Future work should use student-level data, such as GPA, Pell status, first-generation status, and Instagram engagement, to model retention.
